div.head: Becwæð 3.2
div.ab: Do, swa ic lære: beo ðe be þinum ⁊ læt [m]e be minum; ne gyrne ic ðines, ne læðes ne landes, ne sace ne socne; ne ðu mines ne ðærft, ne mynte ic ðe nan ðing.
Do, swa ic lære: beo ðe be ðinum ⁊ læt me be minum; ne gyrne ic ðines, ne læðes ne landes, ne sace ne socne; ne ðu mines ne ðearft, ne mynte ic ðe nan ðing.

Handle wie ich ermahne: bleibe dir bei Deinem und lass mich bei Meinem; ich begehre nicht das Deine, weder Gaubezirk noch Land, noch Gerichtsbarkeit; noch bedarfst du des Meinen, noch denk ich dir etwas zu.

Do as I counsel: keep to what is yours and leave me to what is mine; I do not desire what is yours, neither lathe nor land, nor sake nor soke [jurisdiction]; nor do you need what is mine, nor do I intend anything for you.
Do as I instruct: you may stay with yours and leave me with mine: I do not grudge what is yours, lathe or landsake or soke; you have no need for mine, nor you I devise you anything.
Do as I instruct: you may stay with yours and leave me with mine: I do not grudge what is yours, lathe or landsake or soke; you have no need for mine, nor you I devise you anything.

land ne (ok) lað Nordisch, bei Fritzner Ordbog II 391, beide gleichbedeutend, sonst wird lað: ‘tellus, terra, regio’ erklärt; Toller übs. ‘lea’, das aber ‘Wiese’ heisst und von Ags. leah kommt. Er trennt es richtig von Kent. lathe; bessere hiernach Wb II 129. Doch wäre möglich, dass der Benutzer jener Nordischen Reminiszenz gleichzeitig diesen Grafschaftsteil im Sinne hatte. Sicher nämlich ist so die Formel verstanden worden in den Kentischen Urkk., angeführt Gl II 567 Sp. 2. S. Einl. 2. An Kents lathe dachten Palgrave, Thorpe, Cockayne, Skeat Etymol. dict.; Schmid S. 621 weist dies ab. Abzulehnen ist der Zusammenhang mit Fris. land ne letar (Laeten, Halbfreie), woran Lappenberg und Richthofen Fris. Wb 895 (danach Maitland Select pleas man. p. lxxviij) dachten. ‘Besitztum, Fahrhabe’ erklärt falsch Dietrich Zschr. Dt. Altt. 13 (1867) 27

land ne (ok) lað is Norse, in Fritzner Ordbog II 391, the two being synonymous; elsewhere lað is explained as ‘tellus, terra, regio’; Toller translates ‘lea’, which, however, means ‘meadow’ and comes from A.-S. leah. He rightly separates it from Kentish lathe; correct Wb II 129 accordingly. It would, however, be possible that the user of that Norse reminiscence at the same time had this division of the shire in mind. For it is certain that the formula was so understood in the Kentish charters cited in Gl II 567 col. 2. See Introduction 2. Palgrave, Thorpe, Cockayne and Skeat Etymol. dict. thought of Kent’s lathe; Schmid p. 621 rejects this. The connection with Fris. land ne letar (laets, half-free men), which Lappenberg and Richthofen Fris. Wb 895 (and after them Maitland Select pleas man. p. lxxviij) had in mind, is to be rejected. Dietrich Zschr. Dt. Altt. 13 (1867) 27 wrongly explains it as ‘property, chattels’
